content: ZIP9, also known as Zrtand Irt-like protein 9 (ZIP9) and solute carrier family 39 member 9 (SLC39A9), is a protein encoded by the SLC39A9 gene in humans. It is the ninth member of the ZIP family of proteins, which consists of 14 members. ZIP9 functions as a membrane androgen receptor (mAR) coupled to G proteins and is classified as a zinc transporter protein. ZIP family proteins facilitate the transport of zinc ions from the extracellular environment into cells through the cell membrane. Classification and Nomenclature Mammalian cells contain two major groups of zinc transporter proteins: ZnT proteins (SLC30 family), which export zinc from the cytoplasm to the extracellular space (efflux), and ZIP proteins (SLC39 family), which transport zinc in the opposite direction (influx). ZIP proteins are named for their similarity to Zrt and Irt proteins, which are zincand iron-regulated transporter proteins discovered earlier in yeast and Arabidopsis. The ZIP family is divided into four subfamilies (I, II, LIV-1, and gufA), with ZIP9 being the sole member of subfamily I. Isoforms ZIP9 exists in three isoforms in human cells. The canonical isoform is 307 amino acids long with a molecular mass of 32,251 Da. The second isoform lacks amino acids 135–157, reducing its length to 284 amino acids and its molecular weight to 29,931 Da. The third isoform lacks amino acids 233–307, resulting in a length of 232 amino acids and a molecular mass of 24,626 Da. Additionally, the last amino acid of isoform 3, normally serine, is replaced by aspartic acid. Discovery The ZIP9 membrane androgen receptor was first identified in 1999 in the brain, ovary, and testicular tissues of the Atlantic croaker (Micropogonias undulatus) and was initially named AR2. Another androgen receptor found only in brain tissue was named AR1. Initially thought to be nuclear androgen receptors (nAR), further studies in 2003 revealed that AR1 and AR2 were involved in non-genomic mechanisms at the plasma membrane and were classified as membrane androgen receptors. In 2005, similarities between the nucleotide and amino acid sequences of AR2 and ZIP family proteins were discovered in other vertebrates, suggesting that AR2 belongs to the ZIP family. A 2014 study cloned and expressed a specific cDNA from female Atlantic croaker ovaries, encoding a protein with the characteristics of the canonical ZIP9 isoform, confirming it as a novel membrane androgen receptor. Structure Unlike other ZIP subfamilies, which typically have eight transmembrane (TM) domains with an extracellular C-terminus, ZIP9 has a seven-TM structure with an intracellular C-terminus. ZIP9 is shorter than other ZIP proteins, containing approximately 307 amino acids. However, like other ZIP proteins, it features histidine-rich clusters in the intracellular loop between domains III and IV. These clusters, along with polar or charged amino acids in the TM domains, likely play critical roles in forming ion transfer channels and facilitating zinc ion import into the cytoplasm. Location, Expression, and Function ZIP9 transports zinc ions into the cytosol and is expressed in nearly all human tissues. Subcellularly, ZIP9 is located in the plasma membrane, nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondrial membrane. It plays a role in maintaining zinc homeostasis within the secretory pathway, remaining in the Trans Golgi Network regardless of zinc concentration changes. ZIP9 is unique among ZIP proteins in signaling through G protein binding, and its ligand binding decreases when uncoupled from G proteins. It is also the only ZIP family member with mAR characteristics. Ligands Testosterone binds to ZIP9 with high affinity (Kd = 14 nM) and acts as an agonist. In contrast, other endogenous androgens, such as dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and androstenedione, exhibit low affinity for ZIP9, with less than 1% of testosterone's binding capacity. However, DHT can still activate ZIP9 at sufficiently high concentrations. Synthetic androgens like mibolerone and metribolone (R-1881), as well as endogenous 11-ketotestosterone and other steroid hormones like estradiol and cortisol, are ineffective competitors for ZIP9. Since mibolerone and metribolone activate nuclear androgen receptors (AR) but not ZIP9, they can be used to differentiate between ARand ZIP9-mediated testosterone responses. The nonsteroidal antiandrogen bicalutamide has been identified as a ZIP9 antagonist. Clinical Significance Zinc homeostasis is critical for human health, as zinc is a structural component of proteins such as zinc-dependent metalloenzymes and zinc-finger-containing transcription factors. Zinc also plays a role in cell growth, proliferation, division, and apoptosis. Dysfunction of zinc transporter proteins can harm cells and is associated with various cancers, diabetes, and inflammation. For example, testosterone activation of ZIP9 increases intracellular zinc levels in breast cancer, prostate cancer, and ovarian follicle cells, inducing apoptosis in these cells. This action may be mediated by increased zinc concentrations. Deletion mutations involving the SLC39A9 gene, located on chromosome 14, have been linked to congenital heart defects, intellectual disabilities, brachydactyly, hypertelorism, and broad nasal bridges. Specific clinical issues include ectopic organs, cryptorchidism (undescended testes), and small intestine malrotation. SLC39A9 deletion mutations have also been reported in 23 cases of circulation-related cancers, such as B-cell lymphoma and B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). Faulty DNA replication can result in chimeric genes, such as the SLC39A9-PLEKHD1 fusion gene, which has been implicated in schizophrenia. This fusion protein interacts with cellular signaling pathways involving kinases like Akt and Erk, leading to increased phosphorylation in the brain and the onset of schizophrenia. Another fusion transcript, SLC39A9-MAP3K9, has been recurrently observed in breast cancers. Cancer A 2014 study highlighted ZIP9's role in breast and prostate cancer by demonstrating its ability to induce apoptosis in cancerous cells through testosterone activation. Unlike ZIP1, ZIP2, and ZIP3, ZIP9 mRNA expression is elevated in malignant prostate and breast cancer cells, likely due to the increased zinc requirements of rapidly dividing cells. Brain In glioblastoma cells, ZIP9 upregulation enhances cell migration in brain cancer by influencing p53, GSK-3β, and signaling pathways such as ERK and AKT, which are activated through phosphorylation after B-cell receptor activation. Diabetes Zinc is essential for pancreatic β-cell function and glycemic control. The insulin secretory pathway in humans is highly dependent on zinc. During insulin secretion, β-cells lose significant amounts of zinc ions and require replenishment. ZIP9 mRNA expression increases during this process, making ZIP9 a potential therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes.
